# Mud paint

Garden soil stirred with water into a paint the colors of our own yard. Each bed and path gives a different brown.

## Ingredients

- 1 cup garden soil, sifted
- 1 cup water
- 2 tablespoons flour, to thicken

## Tools

- a sieve
- small bowls
- wide brushes
- sturdy paper or cardboard

## Steps

- Collect soil from two or three places in the yard.
- Sift out the stones and roots together.
- Stir in water a little at a time, then the flour.
- Paint on paper, cardboard or the fence boards. Rain or the hose rinses it away.
- Wash our hands with soap and water.

## Why we use it

Children see that the ground under their feet holds many colors, and they compare soil from the beds and the paths.

## I wonder

- I wonder why the soil by the beds is darker than the soil on the path.
- I wonder what color the mud will be when it dries.

## Connections

- Earth and plant paints and Mud in the Idea bank.
- Compost and the soil in our beds, to compare.
- All year, outdoors.

## Clean up

- Leftover mud goes back to the garden bed it came from. It never goes down the sink.
- Bowls, sieve and brushes. Rinsed outdoors with the hose, then washed and dried. Children may help.
- Children wash their hands in a basin first, then at the sink. The educator checks each tool before it is put away.

# Flower ice

Petals and leaves frozen in ice. Children free them with warm water and droppers.

## Ingredients

- petals and leaves from flowers safe to handle, such as calendula, nasturtium and lavender
- water

## Tools

- muffin tins or small bowls
- trays
- cups of warm water
- droppers and spoons

## Steps

- Gather petals and leaves together.
- Arrange them in the tins and cover them with water.
- Freeze overnight.
- Set the ice on trays with cups of warm water and droppers.

## Why we use it

Children watch solid become liquid and see each flower come free as the ice melts.

## I wonder

- I wonder what will happen to the petals when the ice melts.
- I wonder which melts faster, ice in the sun or ice in the shade.

## Connections

- Ice and Ice blocks on a hot day in the Idea bank.
- Flower watercolors, to paint with the melted petals.
- Spring and summer, when the garden is in bloom.

## Clean up

- Melted water goes on a garden bed, and the petals go in the compost.
- Tins, trays, cups and droppers. Washed in warm soapy water and dried. Children may help.
- The educator wipes the table and floor and checks each tool before it is put away.

# Seed paper

Scrap paper made into pulp, pressed with seeds from our seed library, dried, then planted.

## Ingredients

- scrap paper, no glossy paper
- warm water
- small flower seeds from our seed library, such as California poppy

## Tools

- a blender, used by an adult
- a window screen in a frame
- a tray
- sponges and towels

## Steps

- Tear the paper into small pieces together.
- Soak the pieces in warm water for an hour or overnight.
- An adult blends the paper and water into pulp.
- Stir in the seeds by hand.
- Press the pulp thin on the screen and sponge out the water.
- Turn it onto a towel and let it dry for a day or two.
- Plant it in a bed, or share it with families through the seed library.

## Why we use it

Children see a used thing become something new, and a gift for the garden.

## I wonder

- I wonder how the seeds will find their way out of the paper.

## Connections

- Papermaking and Seeds in the Idea bank.
- The family seed library in the Garden.
- All year, with seeds sown in their season.

## Clean up

- Leftover pulp is squeezed dry and goes in the compost. It never goes down the sink.
- Blender. Unplugged, taken apart, washed and dried by the educator.
- Screen, tray, sponges and towels. Rinsed, washed and hung to dry. Children may help.

# Puffy paint

A salty paint that dries raised and crunchy, so children feel the lines they made.

## Ingredients

- ½ cup flour
- ½ cup salt
- ½ cup water
- color from our dye bed

## Tools

- a bowl and a whisk
- squeeze bottles
- heavy paper or cardboard

## Steps

- Whisk the flour and salt together.
- Whisk in the water and the plant color.
- Pour it into squeeze bottles.
- Squeeze lines and dots onto heavy paper.
- Let it dry overnight.

## Why we use it

The paint dries raised, so a picture is something to touch as well as to see.

## I wonder

- I wonder what it will feel like once it dries.

## Connections

- Sensory table in the Idea bank.
- Garden dye colors, for the paint's color.
- All year, indoors or outdoors.

## Clean up

- Leftover paint goes in the trash.
- Bowl, whisk and squeeze bottles. Rinsed well, washed in warm soapy water and dried. Children may help.
- The educator wipes the table and checks each tool before it is put away.

# Chalk paint

Cornstarch paint for the paths and fences. It lasts until the rain washes it away.

## Ingredients

- 1 cup cornstarch
- 1 cup water
- color from our dye bed

## Tools

- a muffin tin
- wide brushes
- sponges

## Steps

- Stir the cornstarch and water in each cup of the tin.
- Add a different plant color to each cup.
- Paint on the paths and fences.
- Stir again whenever the cornstarch settles.

## Why we use it

Children paint with big arm movements on the ground, and they watch the weather take the picture away.

## I wonder

- I wonder where our painting will go when it rains.

## Connections

- Chalk and Chalk on open concrete in the Idea bank.
- Garden dye colors, for the paint's color.
- All year, on dry days outdoors.

## Clean up

- Leftover paint dries in the tin and goes in the trash. It never goes down the sink.
- Muffin tin, brushes and sponges. Rinsed outdoors, washed and dried. Children may help.
- The paintings stay until the rain or the hose washes them away.

# Clay slip

Clay and water stirred thick, for joining clay pieces so they stay together as they dry.

## Ingredients

- clay scraps
- water

## Tools

- a jar with a lid
- a fork
- a small brush

## Steps

- Let the clay scraps dry.
- Drop them in the jar and cover them with water.
- Wait a day, then stir until it is as thick as yogurt.
- To join two pieces, scratch both with the fork, brush on slip and press them together.
- Keep the lid on between uses.
- Wash our hands with soap and water. Clay stays in our hands and out of our mouths.

## Why we use it

Children learn how clay holds to clay, so a handle or a head stays on.

## I wonder

- I wonder why scratched clay holds better than smooth clay.

## Connections

- Clay and A block of clay at arrival in the Idea bank.
- Clay scraps saved from every clay day.
- All year, in every class's mini atelier.

## Clean up

- Slip stays in its closed jar for the next clay day. It never goes down the sink.
- Fork and brush. Rinsed in a bucket of water first, then washed and dried. Children may help.
- The bucket water settles overnight, and the clay at the bottom goes back into the slip jar.

# Soap foam

Soap and water whisked into foam that holds a shape, then slowly disappears.

## Ingredients

- ¼ cup gentle, unscented liquid soap
- ½ cup water
- color from our dye bed, if we like

## Tools

- a whisk or an egg beater
- a tub or tray
- scoops, cups and our tools to wash

## Steps

- Whisk the soap and water until it stands in peaks.
- Spoon it into the tub.
- Scoop, pour and wash our tools in it.
- Keep foamy hands away from our eyes, and rinse our hands after.

## Why we use it

Foam is light and cool, and children watch it change. It also lets children care for our materials themselves.

## I wonder

- I wonder where the bubbles go.

## Connections

- Water and Sensory table in the Idea bank.
- Bubble solution, for more play with soap and air.
- All year, indoors or outdoors.

## Clean up

- Melted foam is poured out on the grass outdoors.
- Tub, whisk, scoops and cups. Rinsed in clean water and dried. Children may help.
- The educator wipes the table and floor, since soapy floors are slippery, and checks each tool before it is put away.

# Garden dye colors

Color steeped from our dye bed flowers, for playdough, paints and foam.

## Ingredients

- 2 cups flowers from our dye bed
- 2 cups water

## Colors

- Marigold and dyer's chamomile give yellow.
- Sulphur cosmos gives orange.

## Tools

- a pot kept only for dyes
- a strainer
- jars with lids

## Steps

- Pick the blooms together.
- An adult simmers the flowers in the water for 30 to 60 minutes.
- Let it cool, then strain it into jars.
- Compare the colors side by side.
- Keep the jars in the refrigerator for up to a week, labeled "For color only."
- Put the spent flowers in the compost.

## Why we use it

Every color has a plant behind it, and children learn where each one grew.

## I wonder

- I wonder what color the purple flowers will make.

## Connections

- Botanical dyeing, The botanical dye bed and Earth and plant paints in the Idea bank.
- Playdough, oobleck, puffy paint, chalk paint and soap foam, each colored from these jars.
- Summer and fall, when the dye bed is in bloom.

## Clean up

- Spent flowers go in the compost.
- Dye pot. Cooled, washed and dried by the educator, and kept with the dye tools, apart from the food pots.
- Strainer and jars. Washed in warm soapy water and dried. Children may help.
